lessons.title: 01 — Hello, Java
objectives: Install a JDK and check it with `java -version`
Run a single-file Java program from the terminal
Explain what `public static void main` is for
Print text and return text from a method

lessons.title: 02 — Variables, types and money
objectives: Declare variables with the right type (int, String)
Do arithmetic and explain integer division
Explain why money is stored as whole centavos
Write methods with parameters and return values

lessons.title: 03 — Decisions and loops
objectives: Choose between paths with if / else if / else
Repeat work with a for loop over an array
Build a formatted multi-line report as a String
Run the first complete milestone of the application

lessons.title: 04 — Methods and arrays
objectives: Write methods with parameters and return values, and call them
Explain why a method that changes an array changes the caller's array
Search an array for a value and return its position
Split a program into small methods instead of one long main
Show that you can do everything from Week 1 (review checkpoint)

lessons.title: 05 — Strings and text
objectives: Use String methods (trim, toUpperCase, substring, indexOf, contains, split, equalsIgnoreCase)
Clean up messy typed text before using it
Explain why Strings never change and why we compare them with equals
Build text with StringBuilder and String.format

lessons.title: 06 — Scanner and input validation
objectives: Read typed text with Scanner
Validate input and ask again until it is valid
Convert typed pesos into integer centavos
Write input code that tests can run without a keyboard

lessons.title: 07 — ArrayList and HashMap
objectives: Store a growing list of items in an ArrayList
Look values up by key in a HashMap
Replace parallel arrays with an Inventory that keeps products by name
Explain what null means and why a lookup can return it

lessons.title: 08 — Console menu
objectives: Build a menu loop that repeats until the user quits
Connect menu choices to the Inventory (add product, receive stock, record sale, stock report)
Turn failed operations into friendly messages
Test a whole interactive session without a keyboard
Run the second complete milestone of the application

lessons.title: 09 — Classes and objects
objectives: Explain the difference between a class and an object
Write a class with fields, a constructor and methods
Create objects with new and call their methods
Replace the Inventory's parallel collections with a list of Product objects

lessons.title: 10 — Encapsulation
objectives: Make fields private and expose them through getters and setters
Put validation inside the class so an object can never hold bad data
Explain why returning an internal list is dangerous and how to return a copy
Use final for values that must never change

lessons.title: 11 — Product and Customer classes
objectives: Model real things (Customer, Sale, SaleLine) as small classes
Let one object hold other objects (a Sale holds a Customer and a list of SaleLines)
Replace a running total with objects that can answer the question themselves
Overload a method so old callers keep working

lessons.title: 12 — Static vs instance
objectives: Explain the difference between a static member and an instance member
Write constants with static final and static helper methods
Explain why main is static and why shared mutable state is risky
Move a rule to the class it belongs to

lessons.title: 13 — Inheritance
objectives: Use extends to share fields and methods between related classes
Call a parent constructor and parent method with super
Override a method with @Override and explain which version runs
Decide when inheritance fits (IS-A) and when it does not

lessons.title: 14 — Interfaces and polymorphism
objectives: Define an interface and implement it in several classes
Write code against the interface so any implementation works
Explain polymorphism and the difference between an interface and a parent class
Add discounts to the sale model without changing Sale for each new kind

lessons.title: 15 — Enums and records
objectives: Replace "magic" strings with enums that allow only valid values
Give an enum fields, methods and a switch expression
Write a record for plain, unchanging data
Log every stock change as a StockMovement

lessons.title: 16 — Exceptions
objectives: Explain what an exception is and what try, catch, finally and throw do
Write custom exceptions and throw them when a rule is broken
Replace -1, false and null error codes with exceptions
Decide between checked and unchecked exceptions
Finish Milestone M3 and explain the shop's domain model

lessons.title: 17 — Generics and collections
objectives: Explain what the type in angle brackets (List<String>, Map<String, Integer>) means and what the compiler checks
Choose between List, Set and Map for a job and explain why
Write a small generic class and a generic method
Sort objects with a Comparator
Replace a slow list search in the app with a Map lookup

lessons.title: 18 — Streams
objectives: Explain a stream as a pipeline: source, steps, and one ending
Use filter, map, sorted, limit, distinct and mapToInt/sum on a list
Finish a stream with toList, collect (groupingBy, counting, joining) or an Optional result
Rewrite a for loop as a stream and say when the loop is still the clearer choice
Build shop reports (restock list, revenue per payment method, biggest sale) with streams

lessons.title: 19 — Files and CSV
objectives: Read and write text files with java.nio.file.Files and Path
Explain the CSV format, including why a comma inside a field needs quotes
Handle IOException (a checked exception) and report problems inside a file with line numbers
Use try-with-resources so files are always closed
Test file code with JUnit's @TempDir so no test leaves files behind
Make the shop save and load its products, sales and stock movements

lessons.title: 20 — BigDecimal and java.time
lessons.milestone: M4 — The app saves to files (complete)
objectives: Explain why money is not stored in double and use BigDecimal correctly (build from text, compareTo, rounding rules)
Replace int centavos with BigDecimal pesos across a whole application and keep every test meaningful
Use LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Duration, Period and DateTimeFormatter
Inject a java.time.Clock so code that asks "what time is it?" can be tested
Keep reading old data files after a format change
Finish Milestone M4 and explain how the shop saves and loads its data

lessons.title: 21 — JUnit and test-driven development
objectives: Write JUnit 5 tests with the right assertion (assertEquals, assertThrows, assertAll) and the Arrange-Act-Assert layout
Name tests so a failure explains itself
Write parameterized tests (CsvSource, MethodSource, ValueSource) for boundary values
Practise red-green-refactor: write a failing test first, make it pass with the least code, then tidy
Add a feature to the shop (reorder suggestions) test-first, and decide what is worth testing

lessons.title: 22 — Debugging
objectives: Read a stack trace from the top and find the first line of your own code
Reproduce a bug with the smallest input and a failing test
Use an IDE debugger (breakpoint, step over, step into, step out, watch a variable) and print debugging
Recognise the common exceptions and the mistakes behind them
Find and fix six planted bugs in the shop app and six more in small methods

lessons.title: 23 — Git and GitHub flow
objectives: Explain the working folder, the staging area and the repository, and what a commit, a branch and a remote are
Use status, add, commit, log, diff, switch, push, pull and restore in a daily loop
Make a change on a branch, push it and open a pull request on GitHub
Read and resolve a merge conflict
Write commit messages and branch names a team can read, and record your work in a checked file

lessons.title: 24 — Logging and clean code
objectives: Explain why a program writes a log and choose the right level for a message
Use java.util.logging (Logger, Level, Handler, Formatter) with no extra library
Test that the right messages are logged, without printing during tests
Refactor code for readability with names, constants, small methods and guard clauses, keeping all tests green
Complete Week 6 (JUnit, debugging, Git, logging) and describe how the pieces fit

lessons.title: 25 — Relational thinking and ERD
objectives: Explain why a shop keeps its data in related tables instead of one big sheet
Identify tables, rows, columns, primary keys and foreign keys in the shop's database
Classify a relationship as one-to-many or many-to-many and say which table holds the link
Read an Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD) and draw one from a description
Run the SQL practice harness and read the database's own description of its tables

lessons.title: 26 — SQL basics
objectives: Write SELECT queries with WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, LIKE, IN and BETWEEN
Compute new columns with expressions, aliases and CASE
Summarise rows with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and GROUP BY
Explain NULL and test for it with IS NULL
Change data safely with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, always checking the WHERE

lessons.title: 27 — Joins and reports
objectives: Combine tables with JOIN by following foreign keys
Choose between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN and explain what each keeps
Find rows with no match using LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
Build reports with joins, GROUP BY, HAVING and aggregates
Spot the two classic join mistakes (missing ON, counting lines instead of sales)

lessons.title: 28 — Schema design for the shop
objectives: Design tables from a description of the shop (nouns to tables, verbs to relationships)
Choose keys, column types and constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY)
Explain first, second and third normal form in plain words, and when to copy data on purpose
Choose ON DELETE behaviour for a foreign key and explain the choice
Add indexes where the shop searches, joins and sorts

lessons.title: 29 — JDBC: Java talks to the database
lessons.milestone: none (Week 8: databases II; M5 arrives in lesson 32)
objectives: Open a JDBC connection to H2, in memory and in a file
Run SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE with PreparedStatement and read a ResultSet
Close every JDBC resource with try-with-resources
Explain SQL injection and prevent it with ? parameters
Wrap SQLException in the app's own unchecked exception

lessons.title: 30 — The repository pattern
lessons.milestone: none (Week 8: databases II; M5 arrives in lesson 32)
objectives: Explain what a repository is and why the app depends on an interface, not on JDBC
Implement one repository interface three ways (memory, file, database)
Prove that implementations behave the same with one shared contract test
Move the shop's rules into a service that uses only repository interfaces
Run the console app on either the in-memory Inventory or the database, through the Shop interface

lessons.title: 31 — Transactions: a sale is all-or-nothing
lessons.milestone: none (Week 8: databases II; M5 arrives in lesson 32)
objectives: Explain a transaction and the four ACID promises in plain words
Use setAutoCommit(false), commit() and rollback() correctly in JDBC
Make a multi-step sale succeed or fail as one unit and prove it with a failing step
Explain isolation and the lost-update problem, and prevent overselling with a guarded UPDATE
Keep transaction code out of the repositories and out of the menu

lessons.title: 32 — Migrations: the database grows with the app
objectives: Explain why a database design must be changed with numbered, versioned scripts and never by hand
Write a migration file with the V{n}__{description}.sql naming rule
Build a small migration runner with a history table and checksums
Upgrade a database that already holds data without losing it
Run the finished app on an H2 file database and explain how Flyway does the same job professionally

lessons.title: 33 — How the web works: HTTP requests and responses
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Explain what a client, a server, a request and a response are, and name the parts of each
Read and write an HTTP request line, headers, a status code and a body
Choose the right method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and the right status code (200, 201, 400, 404, 409, 500) for a job
Run a small web server and call it with curl and with Java's HttpClient
Say which parts of a web server you wrote by hand, and why a framework will take them over

lessons.title: 34 — REST design: resources, verbs and status codes
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Explain what a REST API is and name its four ideas (resource, URL, method, status code)
Design the URLs, methods and status codes for Products, Sales and Reports on paper before writing code
Choose between 200, 201, 204, 400, 404, 405, 409 and 500 for a given situation
Map the shop's exceptions to HTTP status codes in one place
Test an API against its design table with plain Java, with no server and no framework

lessons.title: 35 — JSON: the language APIs speak
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Read and write JSON (objects, arrays, text, numbers, true/false, null) by eye
Use Jackson to turn Java records into JSON text and JSON text back into records
Explain why the API sends small DTO records and never the domain classes
Set up one ObjectMapper correctly for money (BigDecimal) and dates (LocalDateTime)
Run the shop's whole REST API in plain Java and call it with curl

lessons.title: 36 — Spring Boot: your first app and what auto-configuration is
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Explain what Spring Boot adds on top of plain Java and what a starter dependency is
Run a Spring Boot application with Maven and as a single runnable jar
Write a @RestController with @GetMapping, @RequestParam and @PathVariable
Explain dependency injection and what a bean is, and define one with @Bean
Explain auto-configuration and read the --debug report to see what was and was not configured

lessons.title: 37 — Controllers and services: the shop on Spring Boot
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Explain the three layers of the API (controller, service, repository) and what each one is allowed to know
Write @RestController methods with @RequestMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping and @RequestBody
Answer with the right status code and a Location header using ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus
Wire the lesson 32 shop (Database, repositories, ShopService) into Spring with @Configuration and @Bean
Run the REST API for products, sales and reports on an H2 file database and show that data survives a restart

lessons.title: 38 — Spring Data JPA: from JDBC to repositories you only declare
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Explain what an ORM and JPA are, and what an entity is, with the annotations @Entity, @Id, @Column and @ManyToOne
Declare a Spring Data repository and let a method name become a query
Replace the JDBC repositories of lesson 30 with JPA ones without changing ShopService
Explain what Flyway, a connection pool and ddl-auto=validate do for the app
Compare JDBC and JPA honestly: what you gain, what you pay, and what the N+1 problem is
Test a repository with a database slice test and prove it follows the same contract as the others

lessons.title: 39 — Validation and errors: say what is wrong, the same way every time
lessons.milestone: none (M6 — REST API is finished in lesson 40)
objectives: Put Bean Validation rules (@NotBlank, @NotNull, @Min, @Size, @Pattern ...) on request records and switch them on with @Valid
Explain why a required number is an Integer and not an int
Write one @RestControllerAdvice that turns every problem into the same ErrorResponse
Map the shop's exceptions to the right HTTP status in one place and hide the details of a real bug
List which problem becomes 400, 404, 405, 409, 415 and 500, and say why

lessons.title: 40 — Testing the API with MockMvc
lessons.milestone: M6 — REST API for the Inventory & Sales System (end of lesson 40)
objectives: Choose between a plain unit test, a slice test (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) and a full test (@SpringBootTest) for a given job
Send requests with MockMvc and check status, headers and JSON with jsonPath
Replace a service with a Mockito fake using @MockitoBean, and check that a bad request never reaches it
Write a full-application scenario test that tells one story through every layer
Keep API tests fast, deterministic and free of leftovers

lessons.title: 41 — Authentication basics: who is calling?
lessons.milestone: none (secures the M6 API; M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain the difference between authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what may you do?), and between status 401 and 403
Explain why passwords are stored as salted hashes, and why BCrypt comes from a library and is never written by hand
Add Spring Security to the API so that every endpoint except /hello needs a valid username and password (HTTP Basic)
Store users in the database with a Flyway migration and load them through a UserDetailsService
Test a secured API with MockMvc and with a real HTTP client

lessons.title: 42 — Roles: admin and cashier
lessons.milestone: none (secures the M6 API; M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain role-based access control and the principle of least privilege
Write the rules table of an API with Spring Security, specific rules first and a safe catch-all last
Return 403 in the same JSON error shape as every other error
Add a column to a table that already has rows with a migration, without breaking existing users
Test every rule with a matrix test, a slice test with @WithMockUser, and a real login

lessons.title: 43 — A CI pipeline with GitHub Actions
lessons.milestone: none (M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain continuous integration and what a pipeline protects you from
Read a GitHub Actions workflow file line by line (triggers, jobs, steps, actions)
Write a pipeline for your own project that builds and tests on every push and pull request
Speed it up with a dependency cache, and show its status with a badge
Test a workflow file like code, and keep it safe (read-only permissions, pinned actions, no secrets in the file)

lessons.title: 44 — API documentation with OpenAPI
lessons.milestone: none (M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain what OpenAPI is and why an API needs a machine-readable description
Add springdoc to the Spring Boot API and read the generated document at /v3/api-docs
Improve the description with a title, summaries, tags, a sign-in method and the error shape
Use the Swagger UI page to try an endpoint with a password
Test the documentation against the design table so it cannot drift away from the code

lessons.title: 45 — Docker: ship the API in a container
lessons.milestone: none (M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain what a container and an image are, and why teams ship containers instead of "install Java and copy the jar"
Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for the Spring Boot API with a pinned base image, a non-root user and an exec-form entry point
Order the Dockerfile so the dependency download is cached
Write a .dockerignore and a Docker Compose file that runs the API with a volume and settings from the environment
Test a Dockerfile and a compose file as text, and be honest about what such a test cannot prove

lessons.title: 46 — Deploy: configuration and where the app lives
lessons.milestone: none (M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain what deploying means and how the options (your own machine, a platform that builds your Dockerfile, a virtual machine) differ
Configure the same jar for your PC and for a server with profiles and environment variables, with no secret in the code or the image
Make the application refuse to start with a missing, weak or example password
Follow a concrete, free, step-by-step path to run the containerised API from a .env file
Explain honestly the limits of free hosting (sleeping apps, ephemeral disks, changing prices) and of a file database

lessons.title: 47 — Monitoring: health checks, metrics and logs
lessons.milestone: none (M7 is the end of lesson 48)
objectives: Explain health checks, liveness versus readiness, metrics and logs, and which question each one answers
Add Spring Boot Actuator and expose only the endpoints that are needed
Secure the actuator so strangers see a verdict and only admins see details
Give every request an id and put it in every log line, and switch to one-JSON-object-per-line logs in production
Test who may see what, and that dangerous endpoints are not exposed at all

lessons.title: 48 — Capstone and portfolio
lessons.milestone: M7 — The complete secured, documented, containerised, monitored Inventory & Sales API (end of lesson 48)
objectives: Describe the finished system layer by layer and say which lesson built each part
Add a feature to the finished system through every layer (service, endpoint, design table, security rule, documentation, tests)
Plan, build and present a capstone feature of your own choice with a spec, tests, CI and a README
Present the work in a 5-minute demo and write an honest portfolio README and resume bullets
Explain what the system is not yet, and what to learn next
